title: Volver vs Devolver: Two Ways to “Return” in Spanish

body_html:
Volver vs devolver both translate as “return”, but they describe different actions. Volver means to come or go back to a place: you return. Devolver means to give or send something back: you return an object. Vuelvo a casa a las seis (I get home at six) vs Tengo que devolver este libro (I have to return this book). Add the very useful volver a + infinitive, meaning “again”, and you have a pair you’ll use every day.

Quick answer
  • Volver = to return, come back, go back (you move): Volvemos el lunes.
  • Devolver = to return something, give back: Devuélveme la pluma.
  • Volver a + infinitive = to do again: Vuelve a llamar.
  • Regresar is a common synonym of volver, especially in Latin America.
{{toc}}

Volver vs devolver: the core rule

VolverDevolver
Who or what moves?The subjectAn object
Needs a direct object?NoYes
Example¿Cuándo vuelves? When are you coming back?¿Cuándo me devuelves el dinero? When will you pay me back?

The RAE dictionary defines devolver as returning something to the person who had it before, or to its previous place or state.

When to use volver

  • Volví de vacaciones ayer. I got back from vacation yesterday.
  • ¿A qué hora vuelves del trabajo? What time do you get back from work?
  • Ahora vuelvo. I’ll be right back.
  • Nunca volvió a su pueblo. He never went back to his village.

Note the prepositions: volver a + place (destination), volver de + place (origin).

Volver a + infinitive: “again”

This is one of the most useful structures in Spanish:

  • Vuelve a intentarlo. Try again.
  • No lo volveré a hacer. I won’t do it again.
  • Volvió a llover. It started raining again.
  • ¿Puedes volver a explicarlo? Can you explain it again?

It sounds more natural than adding otra vez or de nuevo, although both are correct too.

{{image:2}}

When to use devolver

  • Devuélveme las llaves. Give me back the keys.
  • Quiero devolver estos zapatos. I want to return these shoes.
  • Te devuelvo la llamada en cinco minutos. I’ll call you back in five minutes.
  • Le devolvieron el dinero. They gave her a refund.

Colloquially, devolver also means to throw up: El niño devolvió en el carro. Context makes it clear.

{{book:the-mind-lies}}

Volverse: a different meaning

With se, the verb changes again: volverse means to turn around (Se volvió y me miró) or to become (Se volvió loco). For the “become” meaning, see {{link:ponerse-volverse-hacerse|ponerse, volverse and hacerse}}.

Regional notes

In much of Latin America, regresar is as common as, or more common than, volver: ¿Cuándo regresas? In Mexico and some other countries you will also hear regresar used transitively, meaning to give back: Te regreso tu libro mañana. It is very natural there, but in Spain and in formal writing, devolver is the standard choice.

Conjugation note

Both verbs change o → ue: vuelvo, vuelves; devuelvo, devuelves. Both have irregular participles: vuelto, devuelto. So He vuelto (I’m back) and Lo he devuelto (I’ve returned it), never volvido.

Real conversations

  • A: ¿Ya volviste de la tienda? (Are you back from the shop already?)
  • B: Sí, fui a devolver la chamarra, pero no me devolvieron el dinero. (Yes, I went to return the jacket, but they didn’t refund me.)
  • A: ¿En serio? Vuelve a preguntar mañana con el ticket. (Seriously? Ask again tomorrow with the receipt.)

Why this pair is tricky for learners

English uses one verb, “return”, for both actions, and it can be transitive (return a book) or intransitive (return home). Spanish separates them: volver is never followed by a direct object, while devolver always needs one. A good test is to ask whether you can add “something” after “return”. “I returned something” is devolver; “I returned” on its own is volver. Everyday English phrasal verbs help too: “come back” and “go back” are volver, while “give back”, “send back”, “take back” and “pay back” are devolver.

Try it yourself

  1. When are you coming back? (¿Cuándo vuelves?)
  2. Can you give me back my phone? (¿Me devuelves el celular?)
  3. Read it again. (Vuelve a leerlo.)
  4. I want to return this shirt. (Quiero devolver esta camisa.)
  5. I’ll be right back. (Ahora vuelvo.)

Movement verbs depend on direction: compare {{link:ir-vs-venir|ir vs venir}}. More pairs in {{link:spanish-confusing-words|my complete list of Spanish confusing words}}.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

If you come back, volver. If something goes back, devolver. And if you do something again, volver a. Three simple patterns, used every single day.

faq.q: What is the difference between volver and devolver?
faq.a: Volver means to come or go back (the subject returns). Devolver means to give or send something back (an object is returned).

faq.q: How do you say “again” with volver?
faq.a: Use volver a + infinitive: Vuelve a intentarlo (Try again), No lo volveré a hacer (I won’t do it again).

faq.q: How do you say “call me back” in Spanish?
faq.a: Devuélveme la llamada, or more simply Llámame luego.
